implementation_notes: Rails ships the pattern as ActiveRecord::Result: connection.select_all returns an object whose columns method is the header, rows is the array of raw value arrays, to_a/hash_rows gives row hashes keyed by column name, and column_types exposes the types the adapter reports. What replaces the classic RecordSet class is this result object; for large tables the materialised form is superseded by enumerators - ActiveRecord's find_each/find_in_batches and Sequel's Dataset#each/each_hash/paged_each/stream yield rows one at a time. Use the result object when the projection is dynamic or shared across consumers, and map to value objects when the shape is stable.
code_sketch:
result = ActiveRecord::Base.connection.select_all("SELECT id, email FROM customers")
result.columns        # => ["id", "email"]
result.rows           # => [[1, "a@b.c"], ...]   (positional, raw values)
result.to_a           # => [{"id" => 1, "email" => "a@b.c"}, ...]
pitfalls: select_all materialises every row: on a large table that is a memory event - use find_in_batches/find_each (ActiveRecord) or Sequel's paged_each/stream instead.
Cell values stay driver-typed (PostgreSQL BigDecimal/Date and adapter-specific types), so JSON-serialising a result without conversion surprises consumers.
hash_rows rebuilds a Hash per row on every call - cache it in hot paths, and remember result.rows is positional, so column-order changes break index access.
